r: The course introduces historical, sociological, and cultural principles behind unequal school experiences, examines how racism intersects with classism, ableism, linguicism, and sexism in schools, and requires a service-learning placement with critical reflection on that experience. The written analytic and reflective essays are exposed to AI drafting, but the service-learning requirement puts students physically in community and school settings, observing and responding to situations no model completes for them. Task-exposure research finds science- and critical-thinking-heavy work less automatable than routine writing, and equity analysis leans on exactly that critical-reasoning core. The course carries a GT-Pathways Social and Behavioral Sciences designation binding it into the statewide gen-ed transfer core. At 24 months, with adoption still uneven per diffusion data, the instrumental need to build this analytic and experiential competence is largely intact; AI can generate commentary but cannot complete the community placement or the student's own reasoning about it.

By 2031, AI will draft fluent essays on racism, equity, and school structures, further eroding the rationale for students to produce that writing themselves. What survives is the interpretive judgment needed to connect abstract equity frameworks to a concrete, in-person service placement, and the capacity to evaluate whether an AI-generated equity analysis is actually sound rather than superficially plausible, a genuine verification concern given how confidently models can misread lived context. The GT-Pathways mandate keeps the course fixed in the general-education core across a catalog cycle, capping the erosion rather than letting it run unchecked. The rating rises to Medium: the written-analysis tasks are increasingly AI-deliverable, but the service-learning component and the transfer lock keep the course instrumentally necessary, with the balance of graded work plausibly shifting toward reflection on lived experience over prose generation.

A decade out, AI will produce sophisticated, well-sourced commentary on educational inequity on demand, and the essay-writing rationale for this course is substantially eroded. But the course was never only about the essays: the service-learning placement requires embodied presence in a community setting, and evaluating whether an AI-generated equity argument holds up against that lived experience remains a human judgment task, especially given the field's documented risk of confidently wrong AI output on socially loaded claims. The GT-Pathways general-education requirement persists in the central case absent statewide policy change. The rating holds Medium, capped by the transfer mandate and the experiential component from reaching High. The honest uncertainty concerns how the course balances writing versus reflection under ubiquitous AI, not whether the requirement and its experiential core remain in force.
EDS 1001.d: The purpose of this course is to introduce historical, sociological, and cultural principles that account for school experiences of diverse groups in public education. Students learn how issues of social justice and educational equity reflect and interact with communities and schools. Students examine racism and its intersections with classism, ableism, linguicism, and sexism in educational settings. This course includes a service learning component in which students apply the material from class and critically reflect on their service experience.

r: Students identify, analyze, and document prior experiential learning against current educational goals, apply basic principles of adult and developmental learning theory, and assemble a prior-learning portfolio that some will submit for credit. The core deliverable, a narrative self-assessment mapping experience to competencies, sits squarely in the writing and office-task category that observed-usage data shows as the largest AI-usage share, and productivity research finds professional-writing assistance already cuts drafting time substantially while raising quality. There is no licensure, accreditation, or foundational-scaffolding constraint on this standalone one-credit workshop; it neither gates a program nor feeds required downstream coursework. At 24 months, near-term diffusion still limits realized effect somewhat, so the rating sits at Medium rather than immediately higher: AI can already draft much of the reflective narrative, but instructor expectations for authentic voice partially anchor the requirement.

By 2031, AI writing tools will competently draft prior-learning narratives, map informal experience to competency language, and structure a full portfolio with modest human input, and productivity research on professional writing assistance suggests large time savings with equal or better quality on this kind of document. Nothing in the course structure, no accreditation floor, no licensure gate, no downstream prerequisite role, caps that erosion; institutional lock-in and foundational scaffolding are both absent here. The instrumental case for a student to perform this documentation work personally weakens substantially: an AI system can competently reconstruct and articulate the connection between experience and academic credit. The rating rises to High. What remains valuable is the student's own judgment about which experiences to include and their authenticity, a residual that is real but narrow relative to the course's execution-oriented content.

A decade out, AI systems will produce polished, well-structured prior-learning portfolios from a short interview or set of prompts, and the central case has this kind of self-documentation task performed competently with limited human input, consistent with real-deliverable capability research showing models approaching parity on knowledge-work outputs. No embodiment, licensure, or foundational role protects the course at this horizon; it is a terminal, elective workshop outside any accredited sequence. The rating holds High, hedged by the possibility that credit-granting bodies still require demonstrably authentic, personally authored reflection, which would sustain some manual drafting regardless of AI capability. The uncertainty concerns institutional verification practices for authenticity, not whether the underlying documentation task remains difficult for AI to perform; the evidence says it does not.
EDS 2680.d: Students learn to identify, analyze, discuss, and document learning gained through experience. Students integrate prior experiential learning with current educational needs and goals. Basic principles of adult learning and developmental theory are introduced as they apply to the student's experience. Students will prepare a prior-learning portfolio. Those who are interested may develop this portfolio into an application for credit for prior learning.

r: The course studies Puerto Rico's history, culture, and educational and political systems through a study-abroad experience that includes visiting and observing K-12 public, private, urban, and rural schools on the island alongside Denver-based sessions. The applied work is not primarily written analysis but firsthand, in-person observation of real schools and communities and direct engagement with practitioners there, an embodied, presence-dependent activity task-exposure research does not classify as automatable. AI can summarize Puerto Rican educational policy or draft comparative essays, but it cannot conduct the school visits or the situated cultural encounter that defines the course. There is no licensure or accreditation lock, and no foundational role in a required sequence; embodiment alone protects the rating. At 24 months the instrumental need for the travel-based observational experience is untouched by AI capability.

By 2031, AI will fluently generate comparative analysis of Puerto Rican education, culture, and politics, further eroding the case for producing the written component oneself. But the course's central activity, traveling to observe actual public, private, urban, and rural K-12 schools and engaging directly with the administrators, teachers, and students there, is not a task a model performs on the student's behalf, and diffusion data shows even fast-capability domains adopt unevenly within a few years, let alone reshape study-abroad pedagogy. Absent any institutional mandate, the rating is held down by embodiment rather than by lock-in. The instrumental case for the study-abroad observational experience stays essentially intact; the accompanying Denver-based discussion sessions on politics and culture may increasingly draw on AI-assisted synthesis, but the school visits themselves cannot be substituted, and the rating remains Low.

A decade out, AI-generated cultural and political commentary on Puerto Rico will be sophisticated and widely available, but the course's instrumental core is the embodied experience of visiting varied school types on the island and observing their practices directly, a task that resists substitution regardless of how capable text generation becomes. There is real uncertainty about whether travel-based coursework itself becomes rarer for cost or logistical reasons, but that is a programmatic question distinct from whether AI performs the task. With no licensure or foundational lock at play, embodiment is the sole and sufficient protective factor. The rating holds Low with moderate confidence, reflecting genuine uncertainty about how the written and analytical components evolve even as the observational core remains human.
EDS 3000.d: This course focuses on the history, culture, educational and political systems of the island of Puerto Rico. Several class sessions will be held in Denver to discuss the before mentioned issues. The study abroad trip to Puerto Rico will include visiting and observing K-12 schools (public, private, urban and rural) to gain an understanding of the offerings, philosophies of education, accessibility and/or diversity issues at said schools. The influence of politics will also be highlighted as one of the connecting threads of the life and culture of Puerto Rico.

r: Democratic Foundations asks teacher candidates to synthesize historical, sociological, political, and philosophical lenses into a personally defended educational philosophy — a reflective, discussion-anchored task activity (O*NET: Interpreting Information, Developing Objectives and Strategies) that current models can outline but cannot originate through lived classroom reasoning. Task-exposure research finds critical-thinking-heavy work like this negatively associated with exposure, even as writing assistance nudges some drafting onto AI. At 24 months adoption in teacher-prep curricula remains limited (Census BTOS diffusion data show uneven firm-level uptake), and the course's General Studies: Social and Behavioral Sciences designation binds it into the university's gtPathways-anchored gen-ed transfer core — an institutional requirement independent of task automatability. Verification burden stays moderate: assessing a candidate's philosophical reasoning still requires instructor judgment, and discussion-based delivery keeps meaningful interpersonal presence in the room.

By five years, AI tools plausibly assist more of this course's preparatory work — drafting outlines of historical or sociological arguments a candidate later personalizes — nudging realized automatability into the moderate range even though the deliverable remains philosophy formation, not information retrieval. Capability trends (METR/Epoch task-horizon doubling) suggest longer, more coherent AI-assisted drafting becomes plausible, and productivity research on writing tasks shows meaningful time savings with quality gains, which could extend into philosophy-statement scaffolding. Still, the binding constraint is not verification burden or embodiment but institutional: the course's general-studies designation anchors it inside the gtPathways gen-ed transfer core, a structural requirement uncoupled from how automatable the underlying tasks become. This keeps the rating capped at Medium rather than rising further, though the trajectory beyond five years is genuinely uncertain given how quickly instructional-support tools are evolving.

Ten years out, predicting the exact mix of AI-assisted versus candidate-generated philosophical reasoning is speculative given compounding uncertainty in both model capability and teacher-education pedagogy; the course could plausibly lean more heavily on AI-supported drafting, or programs could double down on unmediated reflective writing precisely because it signals candidate readiness. What is more stable is the institutional layer: the general-studies designation ties this course to Colorado's gtPathways transfer core, a statutory gen-ed requirement that does not dissolve merely because underlying tasks become more automatable, so the F4 cap continues to hold the rating to Medium rather than allowing it to rise into High. Diffusion research already shows adoption lagging capability unevenly across institutions, and nothing in this course's content suggests it would be an early-adopter case, so Medium remains the defensible, non-overconfident call at this horizon.
EDS 3130.d: Teacher candidates will explore history, culture, sociology, politics, and educational philosophy as they apply to education, schooling, and learning. Candidates will investigate five primary questions: 1) What is the purpose of school? 2) What are the roles of a teacher? 3) What systems shape classrooms, school communities, and the teaching profession as a democratic endeavor? 4) How do individuals and communities influence education, schooling, and learning? 5) How does community culture influence schooling? Teacher candidates will demonstrate their understanding of these essential questions by developing their educational philosophy throughout the course. This course requires concurrent enrollment in EDS 3170, which includes an embedded 45 hour field experience in a MSU Denver Secondary Education Field Partner School.

r: This is a sixty-hour supervised field placement in a multicultural urban secondary school, where teacher candidates apply theory to practice under an experienced classroom teacher and complete performance tasks tied to Colorado's Performance-Based Standards for Teachers. The applied work is in-person instructional support, real-time classroom decision-making, and interpersonal engagement with adolescents, precisely the embodied, presence-dependent categories task-exposure research places outside AI's reach. The binding constraint is a hard institutional lock: Colorado educator licensure requires completion of an approved preparation program that logs mandated field hours, and no AI system can satisfy that clock-hour requirement on a candidate's behalf. At 24 months the instrumental need for this supervised placement is entirely untouched by AI capability; the operative variable is regulatory, not technical.

By 2031, AI classroom tools, lesson-support software, formative-assessment aids, and behavior-analytics dashboards will be more common in the multicultural urban secondary schools where candidates are placed, and candidates will increasingly learn to work alongside them under their mentor teacher's guidance. But the field experience exists to build a candidate's own embodied competence observing, supporting, and eventually teaching real adolescents under mentorship, a formative, presence-dependent process automation does not perform on the candidate's behalf. Errors in classroom judgment with real students carry meaningful, non-obvious costs, keeping verification burden high throughout the sixty hours. Colorado's field-hour mandate does not change within a catalog cycle or two; the licensure clock, not AI capability, is what holds this rating. The instrumental case for the supervised placement remains essentially intact at this horizon.

Even with a decade of capability growth and broad adoption of AI tools in secondary classrooms, the requirement that teacher candidates accumulate supervised, in-person field hours toward Colorado's Performance-Based Standards for Teachers is among the most durable constraints in the state's licensure architecture, and there is no credible central-case path to its removal by 2036. The embodied, interpersonal nature of observing and supporting instruction with real students resists direct substitution regardless of how capable classroom-support AI becomes. The genuine uncertainty concerns how heavily AI mediates instruction during the placement and what candidates are being trained to oversee as future teachers, not whether the field-hour requirement itself persists in the licensure architecture. The rating holds Low with high confidence, anchored firmly by the licensure mandate.
EDS 3140.d: This course provides the teacher candidate with an opportunity to apply theory to practice in order to make appropriate decisions in multicultural urban secondary schools under the guidance of an experienced classroom teacher. During this sixty-hour field placement, teacher candidates are introduced to practices of schooling. They complete projects and performance tasks demonstrating developing proficiency toward performance-Based Standards for Colorado Teachers.

r: Critical Sociocultural Lenses asks candidates to interrogate racial, ethnic, and linguistic power structures in schooling and to locate their own positionality within those systems — an identity-grounded, dialogic task (O*NET: Assisting and Caring for Others framed through critical reflection, Evaluating Information for Compliance with Equity Standards) that resists confident AI substitution. Task-exposure research explicitly finds critical-thinking and interpersonal-judgment work negatively associated with exposure, unlike routine writing tasks. Verification burden is high here: a flawed AI-generated take on racialized power dynamics carries real reputational and pedagogical error cost, which is exactly the jagged-frontier pattern research warns about — users outside a model's competence zone misjudge output confidently. Combined with the seminar's live, culturally embedded dialogue, current realized automatability is minimal, and the course's general-studies and Ethnic Studies & Social Justice designations further anchor it structurally rather than by task content.

At five years, the underlying tasks — critically analyzing curricular power structures, examining positionality, engaging peers on lived identity — remain resistant to AI substitution for the same reasons: they demand contextual, embodied judgment rather than pattern-completion, and task-exposure research continues to separate critical-thinking-heavy work from the writing- and coding-adjacent tasks seeing faster uptake. Verification burden stays low-protective; a model confidently misreading a racialized or linguistic power dynamic remains a high-cost error, and productivity research on AI use outside its competence zone shows accuracy actually drops. Even as general capability continues advancing on METR's task-horizon timelines, nothing in the observed-usage data suggests equity-focused sociocultural analysis is a growth area for automation. The course's designations still anchor it within gtPathways-adjacent general-studies and the university's Ethnic Studies & Social Justice requirement, but that institutional layer is secondary here — the primary hold on Low is task-level resistance, not the designation alone.

Ten-year forecasting for identity-centered, critical-pedagogy coursework carries substantial uncertainty — capability could advance in ways that make AI a competent Socratic interlocutor for positionality work, or the field could reinforce human-led dialogue as pedagogically essential precisely because AI's jagged frontier performs worst on exactly this kind of contextual, high-stakes social judgment. Task-exposure research's finding that critical-thinking skills are negatively associated with exposure is not a guarantee that holds for a full decade, but nothing in current evidence points toward reversal. The general-studies and Ethnic Studies & Social Justice designations continue to bind this course into required curricular structure regardless of how the automation question resolves, providing an institutional floor beneath the task-level argument. Given the compounding of technical and pedagogical uncertainty, and the course's specific emphasis on lived experience and power analysis, Low remains the appropriately cautious rating rather than a confident projection of either persistence or displacement.
EDS 3150.d: The ethnic studies and social justice framework of this course supports teacher candidates' ability to critically analyze systems that shape classroom interactions, curricula, and schooling. It addresses racial, ethnic, and linguistic inequities and hierarchies of power as primary lenses for understanding and analyzing the socially constructed concepts related to human identity and the relationship of these social constructs to systems of formal education in the United States. Teacher candidates will examine their own location in larger systems so they may better serve their students, especially those from historically marginalized communities.

r: Grounded in Colorado's Teacher Quality Standards, this course prepares candidates to design inclusive middle- and high-school classroom ecosystems, distinguishing discipline, management, and community-building while centering student voice, agency, and belonging, with a 45-hour embedded field experience in which candidates collaborate directly with mentors, administrators, families, and students. The applied work, building relationships, reading classroom dynamics in real time, and co-developing a philosophy of classroom leadership with actual school partners, sits in the embodied, high-presence categories task-exposure research treats as least automatable. The binding constraint is Colorado's licensure-mandated field-hour requirement embedded directly in the course structure; no AI system logs or substitutes for supervised in-person collaboration with families, mentors, and students. At 24 months the instrumental need for this embedded field experience, not merely the accompanying coursework, is fully intact.

By 2031, AI tools supporting classroom-community communication, translation with families, or behavior-data analysis will be more present in the secondary schools where candidates are placed, but they augment rather than replace the relational work this course develops: reading a room, building trust with adolescents and their families, and co-constructing a humanizing, culturally sustaining classroom alongside real mentors and administrators. The verification burden is genuine, a candidate's classroom-leadership approach must hold up with actual students in real time, where failure modes are interpersonal, relational, and often non-obvious until trust has already broken down. Colorado's field-hour mandate and CAEP clinical-practice expectations do not loosen within a single catalog cycle. The rating stays Low, tracking the embedded field requirement rather than the pace of AI capability.

Even under a decade of substantial capability growth, the course's core requirement, candidates personally building humanizing, culturally sustaining relationships with real students, families, and mentor educators during embedded field hours, is not a task AI performs on the candidate's behalf, and Colorado's clinical-hour licensure architecture shows no credible central-case path to removing that requirement by 2036. The genuine uncertainty is in how much AI mediates classroom administration, translation, and data analysis around this relational core, not in whether the embedded field experience itself remains a required, non-negotiable component of licensure. The rating holds Low with high confidence, anchored jointly by embodiment and the licensure mandate, a combination that has proven durable across the catalog's clinical-practice and field-experience courses more generally.
EDS 3170.d: EDS 3170 prepares future teachers to design and sustain inclusive classroom ecosystems that honor diversity as central to meaningful learning in middle and high school. Grounded in the Colorado Teacher Quality Standards (TQS), candidates examine how their cultural backgrounds shape beliefs about student conduct, learning, and development while exploring how psychology and learning sciences inform equitable practice. Emphasizing the distinctions between discipline, management, and community- building, the course centers humanizing approaches that cultivate student voice, agency, and belonging while framing schools as dynamic, relational ecosystems. With a 45-hour embedded field experience, candidates collaborate with mentors, administrators, families, and students to develop a philosophy of classroom leadership that fosters justice, care, and collective flourishing.

r: The course applies psychosocial, cognitive, and moral development theory, learning theory, motivation, assessment, and classroom management to the developmental needs of middle- and high-school students, and asks candidates to build the professional skills to coordinate with other school staff and parents in meeting student needs. Explaining developmental and learning theory is exposed to AI, but applying it to a specific adolescent's behavior or a live classroom-management decision requires judgment with real consequences for real students, a verification-heavy task. The binding constraint is Colorado's teacher-licensure pathway, which requires this course as a mandated component of an approved preparation program. At 24 months the instrumental need to build this applied-psychology competence personally is intact; AI can explain motivation theory, but it cannot make the classroom judgment call.

By 2031, AI will fluently explain psychosocial, cognitive, and moral development theory and could plausibly suggest classroom-management or assessment strategies for a described scenario, weakening the pure information-delivery rationale for the course's content. But applying those suggestions to actual adolescents in real time, reading a specific student's behavior correctly, and judging when a chosen strategy is failing, carries real error costs that are often not obvious until well after the fact, keeping a knowledgeable human necessary at the point of decision. Colorado's licensure-mandated teacher-preparation program structure does not restructure within a five-year catalog cycle, so the required-course status set by the approved program persists unchanged. The rating stays Low, tracking the binding institutional and verification constraints even as theoretical explanation itself becomes increasingly AI-deliverable.

A decade out, AI will be a highly capable tutor and advisor on developmental psychology, motivation, and classroom-management strategy, and the institutional cap begins to loosen at this horizon: Colorado's licensure and program-approval architecture could plausibly be revised over ten years in ways a shorter catalog cycle forecloses. The applied judgment of translating theory into real-time decisions about actual, specific students remains a genuine residual competence, but it no longer anchors the rating at Low by itself once the licensure mandate is treated as potentially relaxing rather than fixed. The rating rises to Medium, reflecting wide, honest uncertainty about how teacher-preparation requirements evolve alongside AI capability over a decade, rather than a confident claim that applied-psychology competence becomes optional for future teachers.
EDS 3200.d: This course provides an emphasis on making appropriate decisions to meet the developmental needs of diverse children, with special focus on children in middle and high school. The teacher candidate develops professional teaching skills needed to establish an effective classroom group and to integrate participation of other school professionals and parents in meeting student needs. Students apply theory to educational practice as they investigate psychosocial, cognitive, and moral development; student characteristics; assessment; learning theories; student motivation; and classroom management.

r: Candidates synthesize content knowledge with pedagogical perspectives to design student-centered, standards-aligned units using Understanding by Design, integrating Colorado Academic Standards, High-Leverage Teaching Practices, and multiple assessment methods for diverse secondary classrooms, with a concurrent 60-hour field placement to enact the designs. Drafting units and lesson plans is one of the more exposed teaching tasks, observed-usage data shows writing and office-style content generation as a leading AI-usage category, but verifying that a plan actually serves a specific diverse classroom, and enacting it in the corequisite field placement, requires human judgment. The binding constraint is Colorado's licensure-mandated program sequence, which requires this specific curriculum-design course. At 24 months the instrumental need to build this design competence personally is intact despite AI's growing fluency at drafting lesson plans.

By 2031, AI will draft competent standards-aligned units and multiple forms of assessment on demand, materially eroding the design-it-yourself rationale for routine curriculum planning. The distinctive residue is judging whether an AI-generated unit is genuinely equitable and scaffolded for the specific diverse learners in a candidate's corequisite field placement, a jagged-frontier problem, since a plausible-looking unit built around High-Leverage Teaching Practices can quietly fail particular students in ways that are not obvious without expert review from someone who knows the classroom. Colorado's licensure-mandated teacher-preparation program sequence does not restructure within a five-year catalog cycle, so the required-course status persists regardless of how good the drafting tools get. The rating stays Low, tracking the binding institutional constraint even as unit and lesson drafting itself becomes highly AI-deliverable.

A decade out, AI curriculum-design tools will generate standards-aligned units, multiple assessments, and differentiation strategies with high fluency and speed, and the institutional cap begins to loosen at this horizon: Colorado's licensure architecture could plausibly be revised over ten years in ways a shorter catalog cycle would not permit. The candidate's role plausibly shifts from authoring curriculum from scratch to specifying, adapting, and verifying AI-generated designs against real diverse secondary classrooms, a real but meaningfully narrower competence than the course's current execution-heavy content demands today of every candidate. The rating rises to Medium, reflecting genuine, wide uncertainty about how teacher-preparation requirements evolve over a decade, not a confident claim that curriculum-design judgment itself becomes unnecessary for candidates entering the profession.
EDS 3210.d: Teacher candidates synthesize content knowledge with foundational and topical pedogogical perspectives into student- centered, standard aligned instruction. Understanding By Design is used to develop culturally sustaining models of teaching and learning. Teacher candidates plan and adapt units and lessons integrating Colorado Academic Standards, utilizing High Leverage Teaching Practices, multiple methods of assessment, and scaffolded designs to serve the rich diversity inherent within contemporary public schools.

r: This 60-hour standards-based field experience places candidates in a secondary partnership school to apply content knowledge, educational theory, and pedagogy while making real-time classroom-management and instructional decisions for diverse learners, arranged through the Office of Clinical Experience and Placement rather than chosen by the student. The applied work is in-person teaching practice and live decision-making with real adolescents, an embodied activity task-exposure research places outside AI's reach regardless of how capable the paired curriculum-drafting tools in EDS 3210 become. The binding constraint is Colorado's licensure architecture, which mandates supervised field hours as a non-substitutable component of an approved teacher-preparation program. At 24 months the instrumental need for this supervised placement is entirely untouched by AI capability; the operative constraint is regulatory clock-hours, not technical automatability.

By 2031, AI will handle much of the curriculum-drafting work paired with this field placement through EDS 3210, but the field experience itself exists to build a candidate's embodied competence enacting, adapting, and troubleshooting instruction with real students under close mentor supervision, a formative process automation does not perform on the candidate's behalf. Instructional missteps with actual adolescents in a live classroom carry meaningful, often non-obvious costs, keeping verification burden high throughout the placement. Colorado's field-hour mandate does not change within a catalog cycle or two; the licensure clock, not AI capability, is the operative constraint holding this rating in place. The instrumental case for the supervised placement remains essentially intact at this horizon, whatever the drafting tools can now produce.

Even with a decade of capability growth and AI curriculum tools becoming standard in secondary classrooms, the requirement that teacher candidates accumulate supervised in-person field hours enacting instruction with real, diverse students is among the most durable constraints in Colorado's licensure system, with no credible central-case path to removal by 2036. The embodied, real-time nature of managing an actual secondary classroom resists substitution regardless of how capable AI planning and analytics tools become in the years ahead. The genuine uncertainty concerns how heavily AI-generated curriculum mediates what candidates enact during the placement and how closely the role is supervised, not whether the field-hour requirement itself persists in Colorado's licensure system. The rating holds Low with high confidence, anchored by the licensure mandate.
EDS 3240.d: This course integrates content knowledge, educational theories and pedagogy in a 60-hour, standards-based field experience in a secondary school. Field placements are arranged in a Secondary Education partnership schools by the Office of Clinical Experience and Placement. Teacher candidates apply the principles of teaching and classroom management in making appropriate decisions for diverse learners. This course requires concurrent enrollment in EDS 3210.

r: This course teaches secondary teacher candidates to design differentiated reading, writing, speaking, and listening instruction across academic disciplines for culturally and linguistically diverse classrooms, consolidating the licensure sequence's literacy strands. The applied tasks — drafting disciplinary-literacy strategies, scaffolding language-acquisition supports, building equity-centered materials — map to training-and-teaching and curriculum-development work activities that task-exposure research treats as writing-adjacent and more exposed than embodied classroom practice. Generative tools already draft differentiated literacy strategies and language-support materials competently, giving genuine near-term exposure to the planning work. The binding constraint at 24 months is Colorado's board-approved teacher-licensure curriculum: this disciplinary-literacy requirement sits inside a CAEP-aligned, state-approved program that cannot restructure within one catalog cycle. Verification burden is real because equity-sensitive instructional choices affect diverse learners directly, so a knowledgeable human must judge fit. The instrumental need to complete this required course is intact. Rating Low.

By 2031, AI planning tools will fluently generate differentiated disciplinary-literacy strategies, language-support scaffolds, and assessment materials tailored to individual learner profiles, substantially automating the drafting work this course teaches. Observed-usage data already shows writing and office-adjacent tasks as a prominent AI-use category, and that diffusion into instructional planning is plausible within five years. What survives is the judgment to select and adapt strategies for actual culturally and linguistically diverse students in front of a teacher — a verification-heavy, presence-dependent task AI does not perform. Colorado's board-approved licensure curriculum and CAEP program-approval standards do not restructure on a five-year clock, so the course's place in the required sequence holds. The rating rises modestly toward the base capability but stays capped: the licensure-gated curriculum keeps the instrumental case at Medium rather than allowing further erosion. Confidence is moderate given the course's synthesis role.

A decade out, AI instructional-design tools will likely generate polished, differentiated disciplinary-literacy materials on demand, and the "draft it yourself" rationale for much of the course's planning content is substantially eroded — task-exposure research consistently ranks writing-and-planning activities among the more automatable categories. What plausibly persists is the equity-centered judgment to adapt AI-generated materials for specific diverse learners and to catch strategies that misfire for particular students, a verification role rather than a drafting one. Colorado's licensure architecture could, over ten years, revise how disciplinary-literacy competency is demonstrated, loosening the near-term institutional cap; that uncertainty is genuine and unresolved. The rating moves to Medium, reflecting both the higher realized automatability of the planning tasks and a licensure lock that may relax only at this longer horizon, not before. No confident point-prediction is warranted beyond that direction.
EDS 3280.d: This course brings together future teachers of various secondary education academic disciplines, grade levels, and backgrounds to explore disciplinary literacy and the teaching of literacy and language acquisition in K-12 classrooms, and to consolidate their learning throughout the licensure program. Students will learn about the role of language, specifically the literacy practices of reading, writing, speaking, listening, thinking, visualizing, and representing to gain content knowledge across academic disciplines in culturally and linguistically diverse schools, as well as a hands-on, student-centered approach to prepare teachers who actively promote justice through diversity, equity and inclusion.

r: This is a 60-hour supervised field placement in which teacher candidates design and implement science lessons, prepare and supervise laboratory investigations, and adjust instruction for diverse learners inside a real secondary science classroom under a cooperating teacher. The applied work — live lab supervision, real-time instructional adjustment, safety oversight during hands-on investigations — is embodied, in-person, and interpersonal, sitting squarely in the low-exposure categories task-exposure research identifies as least automatable. The binding constraint is Colorado's teacher-licensure field-hour requirement: these hours are arranged by MSU Denver faculty with partner schools and count toward the state's mandated clinical experience that a preparation program must log before recommending licensure. No AI system performs supervised classroom presence or logs field hours on a candidate's behalf. At 24 months the instrumental need for this embodied placement is entirely untouched by capability growth. Rating Low.

By 2031, AI tools will plausibly help candidates draft science lesson plans and generate lab-safety checklists faster, and that assists the preparation side of this placement. But the graded activity is supervising live laboratory investigations with secondary students, reading real-time comprehension and safety cues, and adjusting instruction on the spot — an embodied, presence-dependent competence no digital tool performs for the candidate. Verification burden stays high because a misjudged lab-safety call or an unaddressed misconception has immediate consequences for minors in the room. Colorado's field-hour mandate and the corequisite science-methods structure do not loosen within a five-year catalog cycle; accreditation-driven clinical-hour requirements move on a much slower clock than AI capability. The instrumental case for physically completing this placement remains essentially untouched. Rating stays Low, with confidence anchored in the durability of licensure field-hour rules.

Even under a central case of substantial AI diffusion into science-classroom planning and formative assessment by 2036, the specific competence this field placement certifies — supervising live student investigations, managing lab safety, and adjusting instruction in real time inside an actual secondary classroom — is not a task performed remotely or automated on the candidate's behalf. Task-exposure research consistently places real-time, in-person supervisory work among the least exposed categories, and the Colorado licensure field-hour requirement shows no credible central-case path to elimination by this horizon; state educator-preparation rules change deliberately. The honest uncertainty concerns how much AI mediates lesson content and data analysis surrounding the placement, not whether the supervised, embodied 60 hours remain required. Rating holds Low with high confidence, since both embodiment and the hard institutional lock bind simultaneously across all three horizons.
EDS 3960.d: This 60-hour field experience provides opportunities to develop teacher candidates' professional and pedagogical skills in a science classroom. In coordination with the classroom teacher, teacher candidates design and implement science content lessons, prepare for and supervise laboratory investigations, and adjust science instruction for students with diverse needs. Course assignments and evaluations are designed to help teacher candidates become reflective practitioners. Field placements will be arranged by MSU Denver faculty in collaboration with local schools.

r: This senior capstone has students design an original action-research project: formulating research questions, evaluating the quality and credibility of prior research, synthesizing a literature review, selecting methods, and drafting a proposal aligned to MSU Denver's IRB and Human Subjects Protection requirements. These tasks — literature synthesis, research-question formulation, proposal drafting — map closely to getting-and-processing-information and documenting-information work activities that task-exposure research classifies among the more exposed knowledge-work categories, and AI already drafts competent literature reviews and research proposals. There is no clinical embodiment and no course-specific licensure or field-hour mandate comparable to the program's practicum courses; institutional grounding here is only the general degree-completion requirement. At 24 months, near-term diffusion into student research workflows is real but partial, and the presentation-and-defense component still requires the candidate's own synthesis. Rating Medium.

By 2031, AI research assistants will competently formulate research questions, appraise source credibility, synthesize literature reviews, and draft IRB-aligned proposals — precisely the tasks this capstone teaches students to perform themselves. Observed-usage data shows writing and research-synthesis tasks are a large and growing share of AI use, and productivity research finds substantial time savings on exactly this kind of professional writing. No embodiment, licensure, or accreditation-credit-hour floor binds this action-research capstone the way clinical courses are bound, so little caps the erosion once capability diffuses into student and institutional research support tools. The residual is defending and orally presenting a proposal, and judging when an AI-generated synthesis has mischaracterized the literature — real but narrower than the course's full content. The rating rises to High, reflecting broadly automatable applied tasks with no binding institutional constraint.

A decade out, AI systems will likely conduct literature synthesis, formulate defensible research questions, and draft methodologically sound proposals at a level matching or exceeding a typical undergraduate capstone submission, consistent with capability-trend evidence showing rapid growth in sustained task-completion ability. With no clinical embodiment, no licensure gate, and no foundational role feeding later required coursework — this is a terminal, senior-level course — nothing in the factor structure caps the rating from continuing to track the underlying automatability of research-writing tasks. The genuine residual is a practitioner's ability to judge when an AI-generated research proposal rests on a flawed or fabricated premise, a jagged-frontier verification concern, but it is a narrower competence than the course's execution-oriented content. Rating remains High, hedged by the acknowledged uncertainty of any ten-year capability forecast and by evolving IRB expectations around AI-assisted research.
EDS 4010.d: In this senior experience course, students will have opportunities to synthesize the knowledge, skills, and theoretical constructs learned throughout their undergraduate studies. Students will design an action research project relevant to their field of study, discipline, and/or profession. The course requires students to identify applicable research topics, formulate research questions, analyze the quality and credibility of research, synthesize research to develop and organize a literature review, select appropriate research designs and methods, and develop a research proposal aligned with the elements and requirements outlined by MSU Denver's IRB process and Human Subjects Protection Program. Students will have the opportunity to present and discuss their research proposals to demonstrate developed expertise.

r: This is a full-time, 16-week supervised student-teaching placement in an accredited secondary school with increasing instructional responsibility, regular observations, weekly seminars, and a teacher work sample rated against Colorado's Performance-Based Standards for Teachers — the terminal requirement MSU Denver must certify before recommending licensure. The applied work is live classroom instruction, real-time behavior and comprehension management, and instructional judgment with actual 7-12 students, mapping to training-and-teaching and coaching-and-developing generalized work activities that sit at the extreme low-exposure end of task-exposure research. Verification burden is maximal: an unsupervised misjudgment affects real adolescents' learning and safety, and Colorado's licensure recommendation is structurally gated on completing this exact supervised experience. No AI system can be rated proficient on state teaching standards or supervise a classroom in a candidate's stead. At 24 months the instrumental need is completely untouched. Rating Low.

By 2031, AI lesson-planning, grading, and data-analysis tools will be common classroom aids that a student teacher is expected to use competently, and observed-usage patterns already show such office and instructional tasks growing as an AI-use category. None of that substitutes for the graded core of this course: sustained, full-time, real-time instructional responsibility for a class of adolescents, evaluated against state performance standards by a college supervisor and cooperating teacher. The verification burden remains extreme because teaching failures are often non-obvious until they show up in student outcomes, and Colorado's licensure-recommendation gate — tied to this specific supervised placement — does not loosen on a five-year catalog cycle. The instrumental case for physically completing student teaching is essentially unchanged; AI reshapes the tools a candidate uses inside the placement, not whether the placement itself is required. Rating stays Low.

Even under an aggressive central-case capability trajectory through 2036, the embodied core of this course — full-time, real-time responsibility for a secondary classroom of adolescents, demonstrated proficiency on state teaching standards, and a college supervisor's in-person evaluation — is not a task performed by an AI system on a candidate's behalf, and Colorado's licensure architecture shows no credible path to certifying teachers without it. This sits at the intersection of the hardest institutional lock and the lowest embodiment score in the program, mirroring the durability seen in other clinical-placement courses across disciplines. The plausible ten-year shift is in how heavily AI mediates the surrounding planning, grading, and data work a student teacher performs during placement, not in whether the supervised placement itself remains required for licensure. Rating holds Low with high confidence; capability growth here changes the tools, not the mandate.
EDS 4290.d: This is a supervised, full-time, 16-week student teaching experience in an accredited public or private secondary school, providing increasing responsibility for the instruction, assessment, and supervision of an identified group of learners, 7-12 grade levels. Regularly scheduled observations and 10 hours of seminars conducted by an appointed college supervisor are part of the student-teaching requirement. Teacher candidates must complete a teacher work sample and be rated as proficient in all Performance- Based Standards for Colorado Teachers to receive MSU Denver's recommendation for teacher licensure.
